stories.headline: Ravens' Lamar Jackson out for game with thumb injury suffered on 1st play
stories.summary: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson has been ruled out for the rest of Sunday's game against the Bills with a right thumb injury.
stories.body:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- Lamar Jackson's return lasted one play.

Jackson, the star quarterback for the Baltimore Ravens, was ruled out for the remainder of Sunday's game at the Buffalo Bills with a right thumb injury.

He hurt his right thumb on his first play in Sunday's game. While throwing a pass, Jackson had his right hand struck by the hand of Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau, who was attempting to knock down the throw.

The two-time NFL Most Valuable Player immediately looked down at his hand and went to the sideline. He went into the tunnel with his right hand wrapped and held by a trainer.

It only got worse for the Ravens in the second quarter, when Tyler "Snoop" Huntley, who is 2-of-4 for no yards, left the game with a right toe injury. Huntley is considered questionable to return.

With Jackson and Huntley injured, Baltimore turned to No. 3 quarterback Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie out of Connecticut. This is Fagnano's first regular season appearance after an impressive preseason.

This was Jackson's first game back after missing the past three games with a high ankle sprain. It's a devastating loss for Baltimore, which had scored only five touchdowns in the previous 14 quarters without Jackson.

The Ravens (4-3) are looking to avoid a three-game losing streak.

stories.headline: Premier League VAR review: Liverpool denied a penalty vs. Arsenal?
stories.summary: VAR often causes controversy, but how are decisions made? Our resident ref, Andy Davies, explains all.
stories.body:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?

For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.

Photo credit: USA Sports, NBC

Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.

Liverpool denied a penalty in close game?

Liverpool vs. Arsenal

Referee: Andy Madley VAR: Stuart Attwell Time: 34 mins Incident: Possible penalty to Liverpool

What Happened: A cross into the Arsenal penalty was nearly headed toward goal by Alexander Isak, but it appeared that he was having his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber. Referee Andy Madley was unmoved and play continued.

VAR Decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR Review: An interesting incident for VAR to check. However, once reviewed they felt the contact fell short of a clear on-field error and cleared the decision.

Verdict / Insight: This incident will be a major talking point, and Liverpool can feel aggrieved that there was no intervention by VAR for this holding offense by Timber. In real time it looked like a foul act by Timber; however, it would have been difficult for Madley to be sure how impactful the contact was from his position at pitch level, and so a non-decision in the moment is understandable.

This season, VAR has been encouraged to set a high bar and not intervene unless an on-field decision is clearly incorrect. The man in the hub on this occasion, Stuart Attwell, clearly felt this fell short of this threshold. However, when analyzing the incident, the action by Timber was deliberate; he made no attempt to play the ball and acted with the sole motivation of impacting Isak's ability to head the ball toward goal, in which he succeeded.

When such a deliberate action has a direct impact on an opponent's ability to play the ball, this must be penalized. In my opinion, Attwell fell short of his responsibilities by not recommending an on-field review and this will go down as an error by VAR in a key Premier League match.

Did Lisandro Martinez deserve a red card?

Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United (Oct. 31)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: James Bell

Time: 61 minutes

Incident: Chelsea were awarded a penalty following a VAR on-field review, and Lisandro Martínez was sent off for committing a second yellow card offense.

What happened: Man United defender Lisandro Martínez seemed to lead with his arm, contacting with the head of Chelsea's Wesley Fofana with an aerial challenge.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty following the reckless challenge by Martínez on Fofana.

VAR review: With no decision on the field by referee Bankes, VAR felt uncomfortable with this challenge but could only intervene if he felt the referee had made a clear error.

Following several replays, the VAR felt that the challenge met the criteria for a clear foul and a missed incident by the referee, explaining that Martínez's act was clearly late, made no attempt to play the ball as he was facing his opponent and not the ball. And, most importantly, that the contact with his arm was a reckless action.

VAR recommended that the referee reviewed the challenge at the pitchside screen. Once at the monitor, the referee agreed with his VAR, awarded the penalty and issued a second yellow card to Martínez and sent him off.

Verdict: A correct intervention from VAR with a penalty and a second yellow card for Martínez the right outcome.

The challenge by Martínez was a poor one; by leading with his arm when making an aerial challenge and connecting with an opponent, there was always a very high chance that a yellow card would follow.

It was surprising that referee Bankes did not award the penalty in real-time, as the reckless contact by Martínez looked clear on first sight. On reflection, he'll be disappointed.

However, credit to the VAR. With the emphasis this season on minimal interventions and the pressure that surrounds their every action, it was a positive decision to recognize that this clear error needed correcting.

Why was Matheus Cunha's goal disallowed?

Time: 34 minutes

Incident: Man United's Matheus Cunha had a goal disallowed for offside.

What happened: A deep Man United corner was headed back across goal by Harry Maguire and nudged into the back of the net by Cunha. However, following a quick VAR check, Cunha was deemed to be in an offside position and the goal was disallowed.

VAR decision: A factual decision to disallow the goal for an offside offence.

VAR review: A quick check with the use of the semi-automated system (SAOT) clearly showed that Cunha's left leg was in an offside position when the ball was played by teammate Maguire.

Verdict: Not a clear or easy decision to make in real time, however the goal was correctly disallowed with the use of SAOT as Cunha's leg strayed beyond the last defender when Maguire played the ball back across the box.

No need for an on-field review by the referee in this situation, as this was a factual decision.

Why did Man United's Heaven avoid red card for two-footed tackle?

Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth (Oct. 25)

Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 37 minutes

Incident: Possible red card for Manchester United's Ayden Heaven

What happened: United defender Heaven flew into a challenge on Bournemouth's Evanilson. His tackle looked dangerous -- it was over the top of ball and both feet off the ground. Referee Gillett issued a yellow card to the defender, with disgruntled Bournemouth players expecting the card to be red.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the on-field decision of a yellow card and cleared the decision as correct.

VAR review: The on-field communication from Gillett would have guided the VAR into a non-intervention as the description of the challenge was accurate to the replays reviewed.

Only a clear error or a complete misread of the challenge would have instigated an on-field review from the VAR. The referee described the challenge as reckless, showing a disregard for the safety of his opponent, and the VAR agreed with this reading of the incident and a yellow card outcome.

Verdict and insight: A correct outcome on-field and non-intervention by VAR; this challenge did not meet the threshold for a red card for a Serious Foul Play (SFP) tackle.

While an area of judgment, the tipping point between red and yellow card outcomes is normally based around level of contact on an opponent. The action by Heaven did tick some of the SFP boxes when considering a sanction, however the fact that there was no contact or any real danger to Evanilson, met a yellow criteria card.

It showed a disregard for an opponent's safety by his recklessness, but nothing more.

Should Brentford's Yarmoliuk have been sent off?
Brentford 1-2 Liverpool (Oct. 17)
Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Darren England

Time: 45 + 3 minutes

Incident: Brentford defender Yehor Yarmoliuk sent off for violent conduct.

What happened: With Liverpool setting up for a corner kick and time ticking away at the end of the first half, Brentford defender Yarmoliuk and Liverpool's Jérémy Jacquet clashed, with the Liverpool player ending up on the floor.

Following a lengthy VAR review, referee Brooks agreed with the VAR recommendation and finally sent Yarmoliuk off for committing a violent action and headbutting Jacquet.

VAR decision: VAR overturn. Red Card for violent conduct.

VAR review: England took time to recommend an on-field review, as Yarmoliuk's violent action wasn't conclusive from all replay angles. However, the penalty-area tight camera eventually gave him the clear evidence he needed to ask John Brooks to visit the pitch-side monitor and review the incident.

Verdict and insight: A correct VAR intervention in this incident, with Brentford's Yarmoliuk committing a violent action towards his opponent and the red card an expected outcome.

Like Rodrigo Bentancur's red card for Spurs in the last match round, when a player deliberately heads at an opponent and makes contact, it is very likely to end in a red card.

The four minutes it took VAR to reach the point of an on-field review is frustrating, as this should have been cleared up a lot quicker -- this will be something ProRef will need to improve moving forward.

Additionally, some discussion as to why the restart was not a penalty kick, considering it was a defender committing an offense on an attacker in the penalty area. However, the ball was not in play when the incident occurred and therefore the original corner restart was correct.

Was Gravenberch wrongly sent off in Liverpool-Man City?
Liverpool 0-3 Man City (Oct. 11)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 62 minutes

Incident: Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch sent off for a second yellow card at a key stage in the match

What happened: Having already received a yellow card early in the match, Gravenberch fouled City's Jérémy Doku and received a second yellow card from Kavanagh.

VAR review: Newly introduced into the Premier League this season, second yellow cards can now be reviewed by VAR, but only if they are factually incorrect, and this situation does not fit this category.

Verdict and insight: Most won't like this second yellow card decision, and it will be viewed as "soft." However, Kavanagh was put into a difficult position by Gravenberch's late, clumsy challenge on Doku, which clearly denied the Man City attacker a promising attack as he had clear opportunity to attack Liverpool in a positive area of the pitch. The subsequent yellow card was not a surprise.

These situations are the worst type of situations for referees, because you really want a second-card offense to be undebatable and obvious to everyone. Technical offenses can be questioned and heavily debated, regardless of whether the referee is correct in law.

Gravenberch can feel aggrieved by his first yellow card. From the replays, it looks like the referee misjudged the contact made by the Liverpool midfielder on Elliot Anderson, and on reflection, a free kick alone would have been a better outcome. However, once a player is on a yellow card and challenges an opponent from behind, as Gravenberch did on Doku, the player is running a very high risk of receiving a second yellow if the challenge is a foul and has consequence.

Liverpool will feel hard done by, but the second yellow card was a correct call from the referee.

Should Man United have gotten a penalty at Fulham?
Fulham 1-1 Man United (Sept. 20)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: Nick Hopton

Time: 86 minutes

Incident: Possible penalty to Man United for a handball

What happened: Man United's Lisandro Martínez felt he should have earned a penalty when he fired the ball at Fulham defender Calvin Bassey from close range and the ball struck Bassey's arm. The referee did not feel it was an offence and waved away the appeals for a penalty.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the referee's interpretation of the incident, that the ball was struck at close range, defenders' arms were close to his body and within bodyline and therefore not a handball offence. VAR checked and cleared the on-filed decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: While Man United might have wanted the penalty, this was a correct on-field decision by the refereeing team and non-intervention by VAR.

This incident is a good example of how the handball law can create confusion in these types of situations. When the ball is struck at close range, the law is clear that the referee should allow play to continue if the player's hand or arm movement is the result of a natural reflex to potentially protect the player's face, and if such action does not make their body unnaturally bigger.

Additionally, if arms are within the body line and the ball would have struck the body/face this should also be taken into consideration when applying this law.

Bassey's reaction falls within this interpretation and was a good read by the on-field assistant referee, who would have led the communication in this incident.

Was Rice lucky not to be sent off at Brighton?
Brighton & Hove Albion 3-0 Arsenal (Sept. 19)
Referee: Darren England

VAR: Tim Wood

Time: 90 + 7 mins

Incident: Possible red card for Arsenal's Declan Rice

What happened: Rice picked up a late yellow card when he appeared to kick out at Brighton's Malick Yalcouyé in an off-the-ball incident.

VAR decision: The on-field decision of yellow card was checked and cleared as correct by the VAR.

In these types of situations, VAR involvement can be triggered only if they believe the on-field refereeing team missed a violent act or an act or brutality. VAR was comfortable that the action by Rice did not meet either threshold, so the check was a straightforward one.

Verdict: This frustrated act by Rice was picked up in real time by the fourth official and certainly high risk, when considering many off-the-ball, non-footballing offenses are often interpreted as a red card offense by referees and matched by the expectations of football, so Rice can consider himself fortunate. However, I am comfortable that this action in isolation was a frustrated and petulant attempt at a trip on Yalcouyé and not a violent act or act of brutality, therefore a yellow card feels like a correct and sensible outcome.

VAR would never get involved in this situation unless there was clear evidence that the on-field outcome was incorrect, so the yellow card was correctly checked and cleared. Rice is very fortunate that the original on-field interpretation of his action was only a yellow card, otherwise he would be serving a three-game ban following the international break.

Why was Phil Foden sent off in the Manchester derby?

Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)

Referee: Michael Oliver

VAR: Matt Donohue

Time: 23rd minute

Incident: Red card for Phil Foden of Manchester City

What happened: City's Foden appeared to kick out at United's Bruno Fernandes following an untidy tangle between the two players.

VAR decision: The VAR checked and confirmed the red card for violent conduct by Foden as a correct decision.

VAR review: The VAR had a straightforward check to confirm this on-field decision, as there was a clear kick out from Foden into Fernandes' body. The pictures aligned with the on-field comms from referee Michael Oliver, and this was a simple VAR process.

Verdict: Foden can have no complaints as he lost his composure in this situation.

There might be some debate around the level of contact of Foden's action. However, when you kick out in nature that Foden did in this moment, it is very likely that a red card for violent card will be the outcome, regardless of level of contact.

Referee Oliver was very quick with his decision, but his positioning was excellent, allowing him all the available information to reach his outcome. Additionally, it was a straightforward review for the VAR, and he correctly checked and cleared the decision having considered all the dynamics of the incident.

Why was Enzo Fernández not ruled offside in Man City's goal?
Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)
Time: 60th minute

Incident: City awarded controversial winning goal

What happened: Erling Haaland scored what looked like a goal that would be disallowed for offside. However, following a long VAR check, the goal was awarded and City took a significant lead.

VAR decision: The VAR overturned the on-field decision and awarded a goal, judging that Haaland was onside before he tapped into the United net.

VAR review: There were two key elements in this offside goal review. First, semi-automated technology showed that Haaland was in an onside position when the ball was crossed by his teammate. Second, the VAR had a subjective decision to make; did Man City's Enzo Fernández either play the ball or impact on Man United center back Lisandro Martínez's ability to play the ball given that Fernández was in an offside position and in front of the goal?

The VAR was comfortable that Fernández didn't meet any of the offside criteria and advised the referee that a goal should be the outcome.

Verdict: This was an incorrect decision by the VAR to award a goal to City, a controversial outcome that will create a lot of noise in the coming days.

What was correct: the factual aspect of the decision, which showed that Haaland was onside when the cross was played. Technology is now applied in these situations, and pictures clearly showed the position of the City attacker behind the leg of United's Dorgu.

However, the subjective element of this decision is where the VAR has made his error. There are two significant sections of law that the VAR did not apply in this moment, which should have resulted in a different outcome and the goal disallowed. It should be deemed an offside offense when (A) A player clearly attempts to play a ball that is close when this action impacts an opponent, or (B) A player makes an obvious action that clearly impacts the ability of an opponent to play the ball.

In this situation, Man United's Martinez was clearly impacted by the position and action of Fernández. Martinez's ability to defend the ball was certainly affected by Fernández, and this should have been recognized within the VAR review.

The process in this situation should have been an on-field review, when the referee comes across to the screen and views the incident himself. This would have been a subjective decision and therefore only the referee can make the final decision.

Soccer doesn't like what it doesn't understand, and this was a confusing situation for everyone. The incident will be viewed as a big error and ultimately game-changing.

Should Sunderland have been given a penalty vs. Arsenal?

Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal (Sept. 12)

Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 54 min

Incident: Penalty awarded to Sunderland

What happened: With the score 0-0 early in the second half, Arsenal were left frustrated as defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland's Dan Ballard after a Sunderland corner, and referee John Brooks pointed to the spot.

VAR decision: VAR checked and confirmed the on-field decision of a penalty kick to Sunderland.

VAR review: Brooks' live comms described Konsa's actions on Ballard as being "all over him at the near post, facing the wrong way." Having considered the communication from the referee, VAR ruled that he was accurate in his description and his rationale for awarding a penalty kick, and confirmed the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: With the heightened profile, focus, and referees asked to be more assertive in set-play situations such as corners, there was a high chance that a small number of penalty kicks would be awarded incorrectly, and this was an example of it playing out in real-time.

From the referee's on-field position, this incident would have looked like Konsa was clumsy with his contact on Ballard. As both players fall to the ground, referee Brooks believed that it was the Arsenal player who was pulling, deliberately facing away from the ball and committing a holding offense -- the type of foul the football world was hoping would be penalized this season.

However, from the replays, it was clear that though Arsenal's Konsa engaged with Ballard with normal contact, Ballard using his left arm to pull Konsa's shirt made the Arsenal defender spin and land on the Sunderland center back. Any punishable offense was, in fact, committed by Ballard and the restart should have been a defensive free kick.

Mikel Arteta was fuming afterwards and it's difficult to understand why VAR did not intervene in this situation given the information available to him, as it was a clear but understandable on-field error by the referee -- the referee's live description of the incident did not match the replay pictures, and this should be a red flag to the VAR.

This was a poor non-intervention by VAR, and an on-field review should have been recommended.

Why was Forest's Williams denied a winner vs. Spurs?
Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham (Sep. 5)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Peter Bankes

Time: 67 min

Incident: Possible handball to Forest

What happened: Forest defender Neco Williams thought he had given his team the lead as he bundled it across the Spurs goal line. However, VAR overturned the goal for a handball offense.

VAR decision: VAR checked the referee's call of a goal for Forest and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal be disallowed.

VAR review: This was a difficult review for the VAR, which involved multiple angles and replay speeds to determine if this goal should be allowed to stand.

VAR Bankes would have been uncomfortable with the way Williams bundled the ball into the goal, as there was very high chance that it had struck his arm. However, even if the contact was accidental, the law states that any touch of the arm by the goalscorer immediately before a goal must be disallowed.

The in-goal camera provided the decisive information, as it showed the ball striking the arm of Williams as he threw himself in to try and score, creating a change in trajectory of the ball and resulting in a goal -- VAR recommended to the referee that he should disallow the goal for a handball.

Verdict and insight: Not an easy process for the VAR to review. However, once you see the decisive replays from inside Spurs' goal, it is a straightforward decision for the VAR, as the law dictates the outcome.

With so much debate surrounding the Harry Maguire "handball goal" from last week -- when the ball struck the arm of Maguire before his shot was deflected into the goal off a defender, meaning Maguire was not the actual scorer -- this scenario is far clearer and the correct outcome is reached.

How new standards cost Arsenal a clear penalty
Aston Villa 0-1 Arsenal (Aug. 31)
Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 9 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Arsenal

What happened: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães was screaming for a penalty after he was challenged from behind by Villa's Ian Maatsen inside the box. Referee Jarred Gillett waved away the appeals.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: VAR James Bell clearly applied the new "high bar" for intervention when he cleared this decision, taking the view that the referee's on-field decision not to award a penalty to Arsenal was not a clear and obvious error. After reviewing the replays, VAR quickly checked and cleared the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: For me, this was a clear penalty kick that should've been awarded to Arsenal. I was surprised it was not given on-field by match referee Gillett, and equally surprised the VAR did not recommend a pitch-side review.

The decision by Villa's Maatsen to challenge in the nature he did, from behind with a scissor action and no opportunity to play the ball was a poor one. By making contact only with Guimarães and none on the ball, there can be little doubt that it met the threshold for a foul -- and it took place inside the penalty box.

The surprising non-intervention by VAR is a result of the Premier League's desire this season to have less involvement and only very clear errors to be corrected, with a new "higher bar" for interventions to be applied.

It's a positive principle that should result in less time spent re-litigating decisions, yes. However, this was clearly a mistake from the on-field referee not to award a penalty and, in my opinion, this was an intervention that has been missed by the VAR team.

Arsenal winning the game will cover the narrative to some degree, however, if this was a deciding moment that cost Arsenal all three points, the profile of the incident would've been significant.

The high bar will absolutely improve the game and lower the expectations from football that VAR should get involved in everything, however it is so important that clear fouls in the penalty area, like this situation, do not get overlooked when the referee has mis-read a key moment.

Why did Maguire's obvious handball not cancel goal?
Manchester United 5-2 Ipswich Town (Aug. 30)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Time: 56th minute

Incident: Possible handball in lead-up to Man United's second goal by Harry Maguire

What happened: The ball was cleared out of Ipswich's box toward Maguire, and the ball appeared to strike the arm of Maguire. He brought the ball to his feet and struck the ball toward goal, where it then took a grave deflection from Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves before going into the goal. Following a VAR review, the goal was allowed to stand.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR, who deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball.

VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

VAR review: With the knowledge that the ball had clearly struck the arm of Maguire, the VAR had two key elements to consider:

(1) Was Maguire's shot on target before it struck Greaves and entered the goal? In other words: was Maguire the goalscorer?

(2) Was the handball by Maguire accidental or a punishable as an intentional handball offence?

The answers to both questions could have resulted in a different outcome, but the VAR determined that it was clearly an own goal by Greaves, meaning Maguire was not the scorer, and that the handball incident was accidental. Both details meant the ball striking the arm of Maguire was negated in law, and the VAR recommended to the referee that the goal should be awarded.

Verdict and insight: It's understandable that Ipswich Town will feel hard-done by the decision.

If Maguire had scored the goal, then his handling of the ball in the lead-up would've canceled out the goal. It's only because it took the massive deflection that changed the trajectory of the ball that Maguire's incidental handball did not result in the goal being overturned.

In truth, it was a 50/50 decision that could have fallen the other way if the judgement of VAR was a different one. But the law doesn't allow a goal to be disallowed in this situation if the handball by Maguire was judged as accidental.

The subjective nature of handball in general is a confusing element of the game, and if VAR had judged this as a punishable handball and disallowed the goal, it would certainly have been a credible outcome given the context of the situation in my opinion -- and a more comfortable outcome for football.

However, the judgement by VAR Jared Gillett was not an incorrect one, with Maguire challenging for a bouncing ball and his arms in front of his body, the ball striking his left arm can certainly be deemed as accidental. It was on this occasion, with Man United the benefactor of it in this situation, and Ipswich rightfully feeling hard done by.

Should Liverpool have been bailed out by penalty?
Newcastle United 2-2 Liverpool (Aug. 23)
Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 6 mins

Incident: Penalty awarded to Liverpool for a challenge by Lewis Hall on Victor Muñoz

What happened: Liverpool's Muñoz charged into the Newcastle penalty area late into the game, and Hall made a clumsy challenge bringing the Liverpool player to the ground. Referee Stuart Attwell pointed to the spot for a late penalty for the Reds.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

The referee: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact."

VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty."

Verdict: This was a correct decision made by referee Atwell and his assistant, and a decision I felt was clear in real-time.

In this type of situation, with an attacker moving into the penalty area at speed with the ball under control, any challenge by a defender must successfully play the ball or they run a very high risk of committing a foul.

Hall was naïve to make his clumsy challenge in the manner he did, and Muñoz was too clever for the Newcastle defender. This was a clear foul by Hall, and a penalty kick a correct outcome.

While it may feel to Newcastle fans that Liverpool were bailed out and gifted a draw after middling performance, Hall's foul was needless and to blame for Liverpool equalizing.

stories.headline: Jalen Brunson joins Harry Styles on stage to cap Styles' MSG residency
stories.summary: The superstar singer-songwriter was joined on stage by Brunson, who presented Styles with a commemorative banner for his 30-show Madison Square Garden residency.
stories.body:
Harry Styles brings plenty of fame to the stage as-is, but the superstar singer-songwriter's Saturday night performance at Madison Square Garden got an extra boost in star power from a guest plenty familiar with the Garden's spotlight.

Star New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson.

Saturday night marked the 30th show of Styles' Together, Together residency, and he was joined on stage by Brunson, who presented Styles with a commemorative banner for the residency. Brunson, who was received with uproarious "MVP" chants from the home crowd, rocked a hat emblazoned with "TECHNO IS MY BOYFRIEND," which Styles has been known to don himself.

"Can you just make a note, we're almost as tall as each other," Styles joked when the two greeted each other on stage.

"And, yes, I will return your hat," Brunson responded.

It's not the first time during Styles' residency that Brunson has made an appearance. The newly minted NBA champion had already attended two of Styles' previous shows during his stretch of performances at the Garden, getting a shoutout from the singer on Sept. 12.

"We may or may not have the King of New York in the house tonight ... Mr. Jalen Brunson," Styles said during the show. "He's just trying to have a quiet night out -- not a chance. Not in this city. It's like Mickey Mouse going to Disneyland."

Brunson will return to his own Madison Square Garden stage Monday when the Knicks host the Brooklyn Nets.

stories.headline: How the Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA title in just two years
stories.summary: When Golden State joined the WNBA, the owner said the team would win a title within five years. The Valkyries did it in two.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Almost exactly two years ago, Natalie Nakase sat across from Golden State owner Joe Lacob for her job interview to become the head coach of the WNBA's newest team, the Valkyries. It was October 2024, and Nakase had walked into the interview with notes on why she would be the best fit, her vision for how to build a team and what set her apart from her colleagues.

But the first 10 minutes of the conversation were led by Lacob: He told Nakase he likes to set incredibly high goals and shared how he plans to achieve them. Nakase sat up straighter and leaned in a few inches closer, enticed by Lacob's work ethic.

Near the end of the conversation, Lacob told Nakase the ultimate goal, the same one he had shared in the news conference announcing the creation of the team a year earlier: "We're going to win a championship in five years."

She slammed her fists on the table in front of them.

"Hell yeah, we're gonna win a championship," she said.

On Saturday, the Golden State Valkyries did just that, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals to win their first title.

Lacob and Nakase were wrong about one thing, though. The Valkyries didn't win their first championship in five years. They did it in two.

"I walked out of that conversation with Joe like, 'I want to work for him,'" Nakase said. "More than that, I want to win that first championship for him."

After the interview, Nakase immediately called her mentors, asking them how she could deliver on Lacob's aspirations. Their biggest piece of advice was to build a clear culture, and do it with competitors who would sacrifice anything for the group.

Along with general manager Ohemaa Nyanin, Nakase set the identity she wanted for her team: scrappy, defensive-minded, no egos. The Valkyries built the team their way, facing external scrutiny nearly every step of the way. People gawked -- or even laughed -- at Lacob's proclamation. But Nakase stood strong in her belief, and in his.

Sitting next to the championship trophy with a beer in her hand Saturday, Nakase was asked if winning the title felt as she imagined it would.

"F--- yeah."

TOGETHER, NYANIN AND Nakase handpicked the players who make up Golden State's roster. During the 2024 expansion draft, the Valkyries acquired Veronica Burton, the gritty two-way guard, and Kayla Thornton, a reigning WNBA champion -- two cornerstones of the franchise -- as well as Cecilia Zandalasini, an Italian national. Tiffany Hayes, a former Sixth Player of the Year, signed in free agency, and Janelle Salaun, a French forward, signed on a training camp roster. The Valkyries used their No. 5 pick in 2025 on Juste Jocyte -- a 19-year-old from Lithuania who stayed overseas that year.

Again, their decisions were questioned. Without a star, and without a history of any success, external expectations for the Valkyries were low.

But in the 2025 postseason, this group made history, propelling the Valkyries to become the first expansion franchise in WNBA history to make the playoffs in its first season. The Valkyries were swept by the Minnesota Lynx in the first round, but it laid the foundation for what the team could build on, and made Golden State an attractive landing place for free agents.

For more than a year, the Valkyries knew whom they wanted to prioritize. Gabby Williams was part of Nyanin's original vision of the team, and Nakase met with Williams in 2025 in Turkey to pitch her on coming to Golden State. But the Seattle Storm cored Williams that offseason, guaranteeing Seattle exclusive negotiating rights with the French national. Williams remembers when she heard Lacob make his proclamation in 2023. "I was impressed, and I was enticed. It was like, this is a team I could want to play for one day," Williams said. "I thought I would finish my career in Seattle, but hearing that made me think a little bit. This guy is not playing around; he wants to win. That was eye-opening to me."

When Williams became a free agent, the Valkyries contacted her again, and Lacob joined Nakase and Nyanin in the recruitment.

"He said, 'This is why we are going to win. This is why it would be silly for you to go anywhere else. This is why we're going to have longevity. I want to build dynasties here,'" Williams said.

"Who doesn't want to come to something like that? We play this game to win championships. I've never won one, and at this point in my career, that is the top priority. ... I was so convinced that I would not win anywhere else."

One day after signing Williams, the Valkyries made another trajectory-shifting acquisition, landing Kiah Stokes after she spent four seasons and won three titles with Las Vegas, where she played alongside A'ja Wilson every day and under Nakase for one year. After Iliana Rupert announced that she would miss the 2026 season due to pregnancy, Stokes started every game, defending Angel Reese in the Finals.

Nyanin knew that these players could unlock a new level of her team. What has surprised the GM, though, is how quickly it has come together.

"You just never know if that's going to work out," Nyanin said.

It has. Williams, who was named Finals MVP thanks to a 30-point performance in Game 7, is having the best season of her career. She averaged a career-best 14.4 points and shot 34.2% from 3 -- and also finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and received WNBA All-Defensive first-team honors. She became the engine for Golden State's top-ranked defense, while also stepping up to be the shotmaker the Valkyries needed.

"The best part has been coming to work every day and enjoying it. Like, actually, that's a huge part of contending," Williams said. "When the playoffs started, our motivation was just -- we didn't want to stop playing together. We wanted to go as deep as we could because we knew this is the last time we could have a group like this. It's been really healing for me. It's made this season really special."

Down late in a win-or-go-home Game 3 in the first round against the Dallas Wings, Thornton pulled Burton, Williams and Kaila Charles into a huddle beneath their basket. They put their arms around each other and took a collective breath.

"It's just one of those things where [it was] an awareness of what we need," Burton said. "And in that moment, we needed to take an exhale and be together and just be present. ... That's pouring into each other and building each other up."

As Nyanin watched from the tunnel -- and as that sigh fueled their comeback and offered a glimpse of the composure Golden State, a team with no All-WNBA player selections, has possessed since its inception, Nyanin knew that all of the pieces she put together fit perfectly.

"That was the epitome of things we have said to them here and there," Nyanin said. "In that moment, all of the little things we have put together, I took a breath as well just to say yes, they will fight with each other and for each other. That's exactly why I am doing the job I am doing."

NAKASE WOULDN'T LET her players pick up a ball for the first three days of training camp this season.

There was no shooting, no running plays, no offense. The first three days of camp were dedicated to defense.

"That's when I knew this was going to be different," Burton said.

Those early sessions set the tone for what Nakase would demand: consistent defensive intensity, attention to detail and execution on the game plan. It also gave her players a taste of the kind of coach she is -- one who plays battle sounds during practice and calls her players "killers," doesn't allow for celebrations, and believes that cursing just means you're telling the truth.

Even when Nakase's behavior seems jarring -- or as she puts it, extreme -- she has built an environment that encourages her players to speak up and feel respected. It's why they so willingly buy into Nakase's vision and style.

"She's so authentic," Williams said. "We know her intentions are to put us in the best position to win. ... She's passionate. And sometimes we laugh at her, but we also check on her ... it's the love we have for each other."

When Williams arrived in Golden State, she told Nakase that sometimes her delivery was confusing. Others have told Nakase that they needed more time to celebrate the smaller wins. Her coaching staff urged her to take more care of herself so she can be a better leader.

All of this experience has led the Valkyries here, to their first title. Nakase's focus on defense made Golden State's unit the top ranked in the league through the regular season -- holding opponents to a league-low 75.1 points per game -- and second best in the playoffs. Stokes had 31 blocked shots this postseason, tied with Lisa Leslie for the most in WNBA history.

And her players' feedback has pushed Nakase to be a better version of herself -- and helped turn around the Finals when Golden State trailed 2-1. After the first three games of the series, she gave herself an F-minus score on her coaching because her communication was poor. So she turned to her players to see how she -- and in turn they -- could be better.

"You can give the best scheme in the world, but if your players don't want to follow it, it's not going to be successful," Stokes said. "Her willingness to listen to us and our ideas about what we think we're best at and what we can do, that's one thing that has jumped out to me; her willingness to adapt to her players."

Heading into Game 4, Nakase inserted Hayes and Kaila Charles into the starting lineup in place of Thornton and Zandalasini, respectively. Charles finished the game with a plus-14, and Hayes added 13 points -- and the change led to a massive momentum shift in the series, with the Valkyries taking the next two games.

"The best thing about our team is no one cares who starts, no one cares," Nakase said. "We can do that because we have a really selfless team, ego-less team."

"She's a great coach for a reason," Charles. "We trust our coach, so whatever she sees, we'll execute."

As Nakase walked out of her first interview with Lacob, she pledged to herself not to let his WNBA team fail. When she began to work alongside Nyanin, she promised her that they wouldn't let each other fail. As she opened up each season with her players, Nakase made sure they had every piece of support they needed.

All of this has led to history, and the Valkyries winning a title far sooner than anyone -- even Lacob -- could have ever predicted.

"Of course this is unbelievable," Lacob said Saturday night as the Valkyries celebrated. "Two years? It's insane."

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Keys to Sunday's five-pack of games
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
Hopefully you didn't have too much candy on Saturday night, because there are five NHL games to watch on Sunday!

And as an extra treat, the entire five-pack is made up of interconference matchups, meaning this is one of only two times these teams will play each other in the regular season. Are there any likely Stanley Cup Final matchups on tap?

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Winnipeg Jets at Carolina Hurricanes

1 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | CAR -270, O/U: 6.5

The Jets started the season 4-1-1, which had them near the top of the mighty Central Division. But in the eight games that followed, they have zero wins and only two total points via a pair of OT losses. The defending Cup champ Canes have been rolling all season and are 11-1-1 in their past 13.

So, the moneyline you see above is not altogether shocking. However, these two teams have already played once this season, and it was a lot closer than you might think given everything in that opening paragraph. The Canes won 3-2 in Winnipeg, and there was some drama as former Jet Nikolaj Ehlers scored the winning goal 6:43 into the third period.

Will Sunday's contest be just as dramatic?

Minnesota Wild at Washington Capitals

3:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WSH -112, O/U: 6.5

Of all the interconference matchups on Sunday -- which are all technically possible Stanley Cup Final pairings -- this one has the greatest chance of occurring, according to Stathletes projections: 1.14% (30th highest among all combos).

Both clubs feature an exciting American defenseman -- Quinn Hughes for the Wild and Cole Hutson for the Caps -- along with a Russian winger who enjoys scoring lots of goals -- Kirill Kaprizov for Minny and Alex Ovechkin for Washington (although he has started the season in quite a slump).

In goal, Minnesota's Jesper Wallstedt has been superb, with a 2.14 goals-against average and .916 SV%, while Washington's Logan Thompson is showing some early-season rust, with a 2.78 GAA and .903 SV%.

The two clubs will face off again on March 7 ... and then again in June?

Utah Mammoth at Philadelphia Flyers

4 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | UTA -155, O/U: 6.5

Both these teams were mild surprises to make the 2026 Stanley Cup playoffs; the Mammoth gave the Golden Knights a good series, while the Flyers won a round over the Penguins before being swept by the Canes. Both teams were on an upward trajectory, right?

Well, one of them still is. The Mammoth are battling right near the top of the Central, with a varied attack featuring contributions from several rising superstars. The Flyers have not gotten out to a promising start; it took until Game 10 to get their first W, and after two more, it's been three straight losses.

Pittsburgh native Logan Cooley scored a hat trick to drive Utah to a win on Thursday; does he have something bigger in store for the other Pennsylvania team on Sunday?

Edmonton Oilers at New York Rangers

6 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | NYR -125, O/U: 6.5

It's the battle for Mark Messier's affection!

Well, not just his affection. Messier is one of 91 players in NHL history to play for both the Oilers and Rangers, a list that also includes fellow Hall of Famers Wayne Gretzky, Jari Kurri, Kevin Lowe and Glenn Anderson, along with Rangers legend Adam Graves and goaltender Cam Talbot -- who recently set a record by earning a win for his ninth NHL team.

Beyond the "let's remember some guys" of it all, this should be a fun watch, with the league's hottest offense making its one and only appearance at the World's Most Famous Arena. Who starts in goal for New York? It might not matter if it's Dylan Garand or James Reimer, given how dominant the Oilers' trio of Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl and Evan Bouchard has been.

The Oilers' goaltending has not been All-World either, so this could be a chance for Alexis Lafreniere, Adam Fox & Co. to rack up a big number, too.

Ottawa Senators at Anaheim Ducks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | ANA -112, O/U: 6.5

After wins against the Kings and Sharks, the Senators close out their California road trip with a trip to Orange County.

While the Sens are right in the thick of the playoff battle in the Atlantic Division, the Ducks are in peril of falling out of contact with the Pacific Division peloton.

And for those who appreciate talented young European centers, have we got a matchup here for you: German Tim Stutzle (with 19 points through 14 games) leads the Senators in scoring, while Swede Leo Carlsson (18 through 13) is atop the Ducks' stat sheet.

Obviously, Halloween is the day on which wearing a mask is encouraged -- and some people wear a goalie mask in homage to Jason Voorhees.

But it wasn't exactly on Halloween when the goalie mask was first worn; it was the day after!

On Nov. 1, 1959, Montreal Canadiens goalie Jacques Plante became the first player to wear a mask during an NHL game. Plante had been practicing with a fiberglass mask, and after he was cut by an Andy Bathgate shot in the first period, he went off for repairs and returned wearing the mask.

The trend would not immediately catch on, but by the end of the 1973-74 season, all NHL goalies wore masks.

stories.headline: Chris Fagan to join the Blues as director of coaching in 2027
stories.summary: Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.
stories.body:
Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.

The 65-year-old stepped down as Brisbane's senior coach after the club's 2026 premiership win -- it's third in a row -- with an aim to return closer to family.

Announced by the Blues on Saturday morning, Fagan will oversee a matchday role and begin mentoring the coaching panel to "establish development pathways for the coaches and help drive an elite, sustainable football program".

Fagan said he was looking forward to making a "real impact" at the Blues.

"While I loved my 10 years as a Senior Coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said in a statement.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting. I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be.

"In all my conversations with [the club] before accepting the role, what resonated strongly was how aligned they were on how to make Carlton a great football club. They shared a clear vision of evolving Carlton into a club that can contend but most importantly, they understand there is still significant work to do to get there.

"To have the senior leadership of a football club share such clarity in their direction, combined with a role that gives me genuine purpose, makes joining Carlton an opportunity too good to pass up."

Meanwhile Carlton's GM of Football Chris Davies said the appointment was an important one to support first-time senior coach Josh Fraser.

"We want to build our football club around good people and they do not come any better than Chris Fagan," Davies said.

"Few in the game have his wealth of experience and ability to connect with and get the best out of those around him. Most importantly, he is a proven winner who knows what it takes to build a consistently high-performing environment.

"Chris and Josh have built a connection in recent weeks over a shared philosophy of putting people first and building a program the right way. With Chris on board, Josh will be well supported, our coaches will be well developed and our program will continue to build the clarity and discipline required to be truly elite.

"We can't wait to welcome Chris and his wife Ursula, their daughters Jessica and Ellen and the entire Fagan family to Carlton."

...more to come.

stories.headline: Tonga learn semifinal fate after pipping Samoa
stories.summary: A late try to Addin Fonua-Blake has helped Tonga beat Samoa 20-18 and secure a World Cup semi-final against New Zealand.
stories.body:
Tonga have claimed victory in a World Cup battle for the ages, defeating bitter rivals Samoa in a 20-18 thriller to set up a semi-final showdown with New Zealand.

Kristian Woolf's side kept their undefeated group-stage record intact after Cronulla prop Addin Fonua-Blake crossed in the 72nd minute to snatch victory at CommBank Stadium in front of 29,411.

Tonga will face the Kiwis in Newcastle on Saturday in what will be the first World Cup meeting between the two nations since the 2017 tournament, which was characterised by the Jason Taumalolo-led defections to the Pacific nations.

Taumalolo was impressive for Tonga on Sunday night but Samoa gave their Polynesian brethren a major leg-up by missing three of their four conversion attempts.

"That's one of those things that happens in rugby league," said Samoa coach Ben Gardiner.

"But I'm very happy with the level of performance, the intensity and the way we went about our business."

Samoa outscored Tonga four tries to three, but Chanel Harris-Tavita and Ronald Volkman could only land one goal between them.

Harris-Tavita came off midway through the second half, clutching at a hamstring after missing a shot at goal and now appears unlikely to line up for Samoa against Australia in the other semi-final.

It looked as if things were going to be straightforward for Tonga, who had the upper hand for much of the first half but only had an 8-4 lead to show for it.

Wingers Dallin Watene-Zelezniak and Jojo Fifita both crossed but had tries chalked off on review before Sydney Roosters star Rob Toia continued his incredible run of form to score Tonga's opener in the 26th minute.

Haumole Olakau'atu ran over the top of Samoan five-eighth Jarome Luai before getting the ball away to Toia, who raced home from 50m out and dotted down under the sticks.

Halfback Isaiya Katoa converted then added a penalty after Jermaine McEwen was ruled to have interfered at the ruck.

But late in the first half, Luai put up a fifth-tackle kick that was batted back to Stephen Crichton, who flicked a late offload away for Brian To'o to score.

Fifita hit back for Tonga soon into the second half before Harris-Tavita flicked another Luai kick out to To'o to keep Samoa in the game.

Harris-Tavita struck the upright with his attempt then winced as he grabbed at his left hamstring.

Volkman was thrown into the action and the substitute No.6 was soon called upon to take a conversion which offered the chance to tie the game up.

It came after Luai and Sua Fa'alogo combined down the left before Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow finished the move.

Volkman was unable to add the extra points but pushed his side ahead when he pinballed through some tired Tonga defenders to score. He then converted his own try, with less than 12 minutes left.

But just as Samoa looked set to hang on, Fonua-Blake rampaged through the middle of the defence to snatch victory for Tonga.

"This group can do anything," Woolf said.

"We left four tries out there - two in the second half - and we've got plenty of improvement left in us.

"We keep heading on the right track but they (this team) can do anything."

stories.headline: Arsenal hold on for a big win at Liverpool, one Iraola & Co. can learn from
stories.summary: Arsenal's defense held firm against the Reds' expensive attack to notch a famous win at Anfield for the first time since 2012. However, there were positive signs for Liverpool when it came to their intensity and effort.
stories.body:
LIVERPOOL -- Arsenal made a huge statement in the Premier League title race by securing a 1-0 victory over Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

A first-half goal from Kai Havertz was enough to seal the Gunners' first win at Liverpool's home stadium in over 14 years. The result sees Mikel Arteta's move to the top of the Premier League table, three points clear of second-placed Manchester City.

Havertz opened the scoring inside 17 minutes, tapping in at the far post from Declan Rice's cross. However, Liverpool responded well to the early setback and were frustrated not to have been awarded a penalty for Jurriën Timber's shirt pull on Alexander Isak inside the box.

The Reds came close to restoring parity late in the first half when Alexis Mac Allister nodded over the bar after a dangerous ball into the box from Milos Kerkez. Arsenal later had a big chance to double their lead when Christos Tzolis saw his low drive tipped around the post by Alisson. Ultimately though, Havertz's goal was enough to secure all three points for Arteta's side and to end Liverpool's five-game winning run in all competitions. -- Beth Lindop

1. Arsenal end their Anfield hoodoo with gritty defensive display

Arsenal just don't win at Anfield. They have not recorded a victory on this ground since Sept. 2012 -- when manager Mikel Arteta was a player. Often they have crumbled here -- think 4-0 in 2021, 5-1 in 2018 or 4-0 in 2017 -- and even last season when there were already early signs that Liverpool looked vulnerable in their title defence, Arsenal were too passive and lost to a brilliant 83rd-minute Dominik Szoboszlai free-kick.

- VAR Review: Were Liverpool denied a clear penalty?

And so they arrived at this famous old ground with familiar questions around their character, especially after losing to Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup, and how they would go about it: go to dominate like they attempted at Bayern Munich, or slip into a more familiar conservative approach?

Their bravery was ultimately rewarded.

Arsenal dug in for long periods, particularly in the first half, but that was simply due to the quality of Liverpool's response to falling behind. They restricted Liverpool to little of note in the second half, aided by a bold substitution as Arteta replaced Bruno Guimarães with the more attack-minded Myles Lewis-Skelly on 62 minutes.

It is fitting that Arsenal went top of the table with a statement win like this. There is now only Premier League ground left in which Arteta has played and never won: Manchester City. -- James Olley

2. Liverpool need to learn from Arsenal's defending

The game was only 20 minutes old when Bruno Guimares celebrated a block inside his own penalty area with the same enthusiasm as if he'd scored a goal. It was an embodiment of Arsenal's unerring commitment to defending, something Liverpool need to learn from if they have ambitions of challenging for major honours in the near future.

While Declan Rice was deservedly credited with a fine assist for Havertz's winner, it was Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson who gave his opponents a helping hand when his stray pass into midfield started the sequence that led to the goal. The Brazil international's distribution has been an issue for some time, and he was fortunate not to be punished for some errant passing against Brighton & Hove Albion last weekend.

Of course, even the best players make mistakes; yet Arsenal are proof of the tenacity, resilience and levels of concentration required to excel in an increasingly physical Premier League. The summer arrivals of Ronald Araujo and Jérémy Jacquet have shored up Liverpool's defence, but Arsenal are still the gold standard when it comes to shutting teams out and they continue to prove that while goals win you games, it is defence that wins you titles. -- Lindop

3. Humble Havertz outshines Liverpool's all-star attack

It is perhaps unfair to suggest that a Champions League winner -- and somebody who scored the winning goal no less -- like Havertz is not a star in his own right. After all, his goal here made him the Premier League's all-time leading goalscorer from Germany on 46, surpassing Ilkay Gündogan. But Arsenal signed Viktor Gyökeres in 2025 because they felt they needed an upgrade in the centre-forward position while also scouring the market this summer in the hope Julián Álvarez, Morgan Rogers or Julian Alvarez might bolster their attack.

Contrast that with Liverpool's front four on Sunday: Alexander Isak (£125m), Bradley Barcola (£123m), Florian Wirtz (£116.5m) and Cody Gakpo (£37m) cost a combined £401.5m in transfer fees. Arsenal's quartet of Havertz (£67.5m), Martin Odegaard (£34m), Christos Tzolis (£34m) and Noni Madueke (£52m) cost £187.5m. Price tags are no guarantee of success, but there is an irony in a team that craved a big money attacker beating the side that has made several, and keeping a clean sheer in the process.

This wasn't a scintillating attacking display, but a combination of power, guile and fight that made the difference, and Havertz has another big goal to add to his collection. -- Olley

4. Finally, the intensity is back at Liverpool

The majority of the noise towards the end of Sunday's game was emanating from the away fans, who taunted the Anfield crowd with defiant chants of "Campeones."

With Liverpool now nine points adrift of Arteta's side, it seems unlikely they will reclaim their Premier League crown this term. However, once the dust has settled on a disappointing defeat, Reds' supporters will reflect on plenty of positives from their team, who dominated for large periods against the reigning champions.

After Arsenal took an early lead, Liverpool went through the gears and put their visitors under enormous pressure. They went into the break having had 28 touches in the opposition box --- the most on record (since 2008-09) by any side in the first half of a Premier League game against Arsenal.

Considering the wealth of expensive attacking talent at their disposal, Liverpool will be disappointed that they did not register a single shot on target, and the quality of their chances diminished in the second half. However, the noise inside Anfield as the hosts pushed for an equaliser spoke of a crowd who believe their team are at the beginning of a potentially special process under manager Andoni Iraola, whose dynamic, front-footed style is already very popular on Merseyside. -- Lindop

Formula 1 heads to Mexico on a weekend where Kimi Antonelli could win the drivers' championship for the first time.

The Mercedes driver extended his lead in the title to 123 points from George Russell after winning the United States Grand Prix. He will simply need to finish ninth or higher in Mexico City to seal the title.

It's a true anomaly on the calendar due to the high altitude of of 7,300 feet (2,200 metres) and therefore presents a unique challenge for the teams and drivers. Teams can run Monaco-level downforce packages while still reaching Monza-esque top speeds.

Norris pulled out a thrilling lap to take pole position in Mexico, his first pole since the Belgian Grand Prix in July. The Brit said on the team radio afterwards "What a lap. What a lap. Even I don't know how I did that."

Who will win this year?

Antonelli put his Mercedes on a surprise pole in Austin and converted it into another victory as he inches closer to taking the title crown with five races remaining.

The youngster will need just two points this weekend, or for Russell and Hamilton to not win the race, to get the job done in Mexico.

Red Bull are a looming threat each weekend after bringing major upgrades and Verstappen will be one to watch out for. He's also got five race victories under his belt around Mexico City.

All eyes will be on Antonelli. He will be hoping to wrap up the title and is looking like he's in a position where nobody will be able to stop him.

What you need to know for Sunday

Tighter lines suggest the potential for close games, a welcome environment for fantasy purposes given the greater predictability of playing time and workloads when games are tight and coaching patterns remain steadier.

The action opens with the Orlando Magic hosting the Boston Celtics in a matinee. We won't see Boston's Mitchell Robinson due to planned rest, while Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs are sidelined for the Magic. Learn about a rising two-way Magic guard in the streaming section below.

The Indiana Pacers host the Brooklyn Nets in a contest with a lengthy injury report. The absence of Tyrese Haliburton and Ivica Zubac for the Pacers spells another big role for combo guard Andrew Nembhard. Third-year forward Jarace Walker could help in deeper leagues thanks to his ability to do a little bit of everything.

The LA Clippers' decline includes being underdogs to a Golden State Warriors team that won't have Stephen Curry or Draymond Green due to respective injury-management plans. This all points to a big role for Yaxel Lendeborg, who has proven to be one of the most productive rookies in an already impressive class.

The slate concludes with the Los Angeles Lakers hosting the Toronto Raptors. Kawhi Leonard's knee issues resurfaced recently, putting the offense back in the hands of Scottie Barnes. The Lakers are looking to make up for Friday's embarrassing loss to the Warriors and should field a full roster.

With an eye toward uncovering compelling betting angles and fantasy decisions, let's take a look at the day ahead in the NBA.

Anthony Black, PG/SG, Magic (rostered in 43.3% of ESPN leagues)
Last season, it took a series of injuries to high-usage teammates for Black to emerge as a difference-making statistical force. With Banchero and Suggs both sitting, Black is back in pole position to produce. Among the league leaders in drives when he was initiating offense for Orlando last spring, there are several paths to impressive numbers for Black this afternoon.

Isaiah Jackson, PF/C, Clippers (11.3%)
The Clippers are using a committee of forwards to handle frontcourt duties this season. Jackson is emerging from the crowd with active defensive play and helpful, connective passing from the high post. He's due to earn over 20 minutes of run against smaller Golden State lineups, so Jackson has real upside during this quiet Sunday slate.

De'Anthony Melton, PG/SG, Warriors (8.9%)
Another player with the potential to post stocks (steals and blocks) in bunches, Melton can become a valuable plug-and-play option during these games without Curry. Even the absence of Green is a factor in Melton's endorsement as the team's backcourt will need to generate for others without Green running the half-court engine.

Anthony Black OVER 13.5 points (-112)

Drives often consume possessions that end in a shot attempt, foul, pass, or turnover. Black is a deft driver with real size who could play well against Boston's backcourt. The only game Black hasn't gone over this number was due to his earning four fouls early, last week against the Toronto Raptors. All of the requisite opportunity rates are present for Black to get buckets.

Pacing the Warriors with 14.2 rebounding chances per game, Lendeborg's potential rebounds should spike even more today with Green absent from the lineup. The Clippers don't have any dominant rebounders on their roster, aiding this rookie's pursuit on the glass. Likely to lead the team in minutes, Lendeborg is in a good spot to not only hit this threshold, but also to merit interest in double-double (+210) outcomes, as well.
